newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW-AIB silent on share buyback.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-AIB silent on share buyback.

text.p: Allied Irish Banks Plc on Thursday would not comment on whether it had any plans to exercise its option to buy back up to 50 million of its own shares.

AIB has shareholder approval to buy back the shares from the U.S. shareholders of Dauphin Deposit Corp who opted for shares rather than cash in AIB's recent $1.36 billion acquisition of the U.S. bank.
Kevin Kelly, managing director of AIB Bank, said he couldn't comment on the share buyback but noted that 85 percent of Dauphin shares were exchanged for AIB American Depositary Receipts (ADRs).
He said there had been little evidence of selling of those shares.
There had been some concern in the market that if Dauphin shareholders, who now own around 19 percent of total AIB shares, moved to sell, it would depress the AIB share price.
He said AIB's primary focus in the short-term would be on integrating Dauphin but it didn't have a closed mind in relation to further acquisitions.

The bank remains on the lookout for acquisitions in the mid-Atlantic area of the U.S., where Dauphin and AIB's U.S. bank First Maryland Bancorp operate, and continues to keep an eye on opportunities in the UK, Kelly said.

He said he would not rule out a further acquisition in Eastern Europe but while the bank kept an eye on developments in four or five East European countries, including Hungary and the Czech Republic, its main focus at the moment was on Poland.
"It's a very attractive market with a population of nearly 40 million," Kelly said.
AIB holds a 60 percent stake in Wielkopolski Bank Kredytowy (WBK) although it has no plans to further raise its stake at this point.
Kelly said four of WBK's 90 branches were affected by recent severe flooding in Poland but it was too early to predict the overall effect on the bank.

AIB, which earlier announced a 20 percent rise in half-year pre-tax profits to 242.2 million Irish pounds, said loan growth in the Republic of Ireland remained very strong after growing by 10.3 percent in the first half.
"At present demand is still there, it's still strong. There are no signs of it tailing off," Kelly said.
